title: Function Composition Challenge
story: You're designing a factory assembly line. Raw material enters, Machine A doubles it, Machine B adds ten, Machine C halves it. Each machine is a function — and the final product is the result of chaining them all together.
why: Function composition — feeding one function's output into another's input — is how complex programs are built from simple, single-purpose building blocks.
analogy: Function composition is like a factory assembly line. A raw metal sheet enters Station 1 (cutting), the cut piece goes to Station 2 (painting), the painted piece goes to Station 3 (packaging). Each station is a function. Rearrange the stations and you get a different product.
try_it: Add a fifth function `triple(x: Int) -> Int` and insert it between `square` and `halve`. Then try a completely different order and predict the result before running.
tips: Each intermediate variable (step1, step2, step3) holds the state at that point in the pipeline
The order of functions changes the final result — math isn't always commutative
Name intermediate variables descriptively: step1, step2 or doubled, with_ten, halved
Each function only knows about its input — it has no idea it's part of a chain
common_mistakes: Skipping an intermediate variable and trying to feed an undefined value to the next function
Assuming order doesn't matter — double then halve is different from halve then double with integers
Writing one giant function instead of composing small ones together
